out.other_title: Debate helps non-expert LLM and human judges on QuALITY; persuasive debaters help more
out.rationale: The authors confirm judge positional bias but find that Khan et al.'s recommended remedy, presenting each question twice with answer and debating order swapped, gives no significant difference in mean judge accuracy and only a minor reduction in variance. The target record reports that debate helps non-expert models and humans on QuALITY, at 76% and 88% accuracy against naive baselines of 48% and 60%, and does not state the both-orders recommendation. The ablation does not test whether debate helps judges, and the target's result does not bear on whether judging in both orders changes accuracy, so neither bears on the other's claim. The citing passage names the cited work, but the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result, so the link proposes only SHARES_TOPIC as navigation context.
out.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: Judge accuracy in debates between LLMs; the source tests whether judging in both answer orders improves mean judge accuracy relative to a randomised single order, on the authors' own balanced datasets with LLM judge models across debate and other protocols, while the target reports how much debate raises the accuracy of non-expert models and humans on QuALITY

text: Khan et al. report positional bias in judges and recommend judging each question in both answer orders, doubling cost. The authors find judges are positionally biased, but using both orders gives no significant difference in mean judge accuracy and only reduces variance, suggesting randomising the answer position is sufficient.
title: Kenton et al. find Khan et al.'s both-orders judging gives no accuracy gain over randomised order
